title: Why Every AI Chip Needs SK Hynix? HBM Memory Explained
core_paradox: SK Hynix turned a 2013 gaming memory gamble that Samsung abandoned in 2019 into AI's ultimate bottleneck — at the cost of devouring 3x the wafer space per gigabyte and tying its HBM4 future to custom foundry silicon.

thumbnail.headline: SOLD OUT
thumbnail.visual_prompt: 2D flat cel-shaded comic illustration of a tech CEO in black leather jacket holding an empty green AI GPU board reaching across a barrier gate toward a glowing golden 3D-stacked HBM chip tower guarded by a smiling semiconductor engineer in white lab coat, bold black ink outlines, vivid blue and gold contrast

seo.summary_hook:
Nvidia builds the fastest AI GPUs on earth, yet thirty-thousand-dollar racks still wait on tiny vertical memory cubes from South Korea's SK Hynix. Even crazier: rival memory giant Samsung helped pioneer HBM — then disbanded its core HBM team in 2019 right before AI changed computing forever.

Here is the 13-year story of how AMD's 2013 skyscraper gamble, liquid MR-MUF underfill, and TSMC CoWoS turned SK Hynix into AI's kingmaker — and why every gigabyte of HBM eats 3x the silicon wafer of normal RAM.
learning_bullets: Why AMD & SK Hynix built the first 3D-stacked HBM chip in 2013 — and why Samsung walked away in 2019
The Memory Wall: why 10,000 GPU cores starve behind a 64-bit bus vs. HBM's 1,024-bit vertical TSV elevators
The Glue War: how SK Hynix's liquid MR-MUF beat TC-NCF film on 12-layer HBM3E heat and yields
The 3x Wafer Tradeoff: how HBM cannibalized DDR5 capacity and why HBM4 binds SK Hynix to TSMC

long_scenes.narration: Nvidia designs the most sought-after AI processor on the planet.
Tech giants wire tens of billions of dollars just to reserve future racks.
Yet inside brand-new data centers, rows of thirty-thousand-dollar servers sit waiting.
Not because Nvidia forgot how to design silicon.
They are waiting on tiny stacked memory cubes sitting millimeter-close beside the processor.
Those cubes are called High Bandwidth Memory, or HBM.
And over half of the world's AI supply comes from one South Korean underdog: SK Hynix.

long_scenes.narration: For nearly ten years, that bet looked like an expensive commercial dead end.
Gamers didn't want to pay extra for exotic stacked silicon.
Then ChatGPT arrived, and overnight every AI lab hit the exact same physical wall.
Nvidia locked up SK Hynix's entire HBM calendar a full year before chips even left the fab.
When Samsung rushed back in, its twelve-layer stacks ran into brutal heat and yield traps.
Even wilder, every gigabyte of HBM devours roughly three times the wafer space of normal RAM.

long_scenes.narration: So feeding AI servers started starving laptops, phones, and cloud memory worldwide.
One forgotten gaming experiment quietly became the tollbooth of artificial intelligence.
Why can't the fastest GPU on earth think without stacked memory right beside it?
How did liquid glue give SK Hynix a multi-year manufacturing lead over Samsung?
And why does SK Hynix's biggest victory now force a dangerous new dependency on TSMC?
To understand how SK Hynix cornered AI, we have to go back to a desperate GPU gamble in 2013.
It is 2013, and graphics chip engineers at AMD are staring at a circuit board problem.
Every generation, GPU cores get faster, demanding wider rivers of data every millisecond.
With traditional GDDR5 memory, you surround the processor with a flat ring of memory chips.
Push clock speeds higher across inches of copper, and memory alone burns dozens of watts.
So AMD sketches a radical alternative: stop spreading memory outward and build a skyscraper.
AMD brings that skyscraper proposal to memory makers, looking for a manufacturing partner.
To giant commodity DRAM fabs, drilling vertical holes through thinned silicon looks insane.
PCs and phones buy billions of cheap flat chips; nobody is asking for pricey 3D towers.
SK Hynix, forever playing catch-up behind Samsung in DRAM, decides to take the risk.
In late 2013, SK Hynix produces the world's first working HBM memory cube.
long_scenes.citation_note: Wikipedia [S1]: SK Hynix produced the first HBM chip in 2013

long_scenes.narration: Two years later, AMD ships it inside the Radeon Fury graphics card.
long_scenes.citation_note: Wikipedia [S1] & HN [S8]: AMD Fiji shipped first HBM in 2015

long_scenes.narration: Technically, it is a marvel, packing a 1,024-bit interface per stack onto a tiny card.
Commercially, for consumer gaming cards, the silicon interposer costs way too much.
Nvidia sticks with cheaper GDDR5X on gaming cards and crushes AMD in retail sales.
Inside Samsung's headquarters, finance teams look at tiny HBM shipments and pull the plug.
Why burn cleanroom engineers on niche supercomputer memory when phone DRAM prints billions?
Yet inside SK Hynix, engineers quietly keep iterating: HBM2, HBM2E, then HBM3.
Every generation teaches SK Hynix painful lessons about wafer thinning, heat, and warpage.
Lessons nobody cared about, until large language models broke computer architecture.

long_scenes.narration: Traditional DDR5 memory uses a narrow 64-bit bus clocked faster and faster.
HBM flips the physics completely: lower the clock speed, but make the highway ultra-wide.
First, engineers grind each silicon DRAM wafer down until it is thinner than a human hair.
Next, they stack eight, twelve, or sixteen memory dies directly on top of a base logic die.
Then lasers and chemical etching drill thousands of microscopic copper elevators called TSVs.
Instead of traveling centimeters across fiberglass, data drops microns straight into a silicon interposer.
Hardware benchmarks on early two-stack HBM FPGAs already measured 425 gigabytes per second.

long_scenes.narration: That is why cloud CEOs happily pay whatever SK Hynix asks for taller, denser HBM3E towers.
Which raises the obvious question: once AI exploded, why couldn't Samsung instantly catch up?
The secret weapon wasn't lithography—it was how you glue twelve hot chips together.
Samsung relied on TC-NCF: laying thin solid non-conductive film between every single layer.
Each layer had to be heat-pressed down under high force, risking micro-cracks and trapped heat.
At four or eight layers, solid film worked fine; at twelve layers, yields and thermals suffered.
SK Hynix spent years perfecting MR-MUF: Mass Reflow with Molded Underfill.
Instead of pressing layers one by one, SK Hynix melts all micro-bumps simultaneously in one oven cycle.
Then a specialty liquid protective resin flows into every microscopic gap and hardens.
Better cooling meant cleaner Nvidia qualification, higher yields, and first-mover HBM3E profits.
From South Korea, finished HBM cubes fly straight to TSMC's advanced packaging fabs in Taiwan.
Inside TSMC's CoWoS line, robots place Nvidia's GPU beside six or eight SK Hynix HBM stacks.
If either SK Hynix's memory yield or TSMC's CoWoS interposer capacity slows down, everything stops.
Even worse, once bonded onto a CoWoS interposer, a bad stack cannot simply be unplugged.
Reliability became priceless, letting SK Hynix demand upfront cash prepayments and premium margins.
But every engineering triumph in semiconductors comes with an unforgiving tradeoff.
Thousands of TSV elevator shafts punch right through silicon real estate that normally stores bits.
Add wider buses and stacking yield losses, and one gigabyte of HBM eats three gigabytes of DDR5 wafer.
long_scenes.citation_note: Wikipedia [S3]: HBM wafer allocation & global memory supply shortage

long_scenes.narration: Building a new cleanroom fab takes years and tens of billions of dollars.
So SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron converted existing standard DRAM lines into HBM lines.
The result was the global memory crunch starting in 2025, lifting prices for everyday electronics.
And SK Hynix faces an even deeper strategic tradeoff with next-generation HBM4.
Until now, SK Hynix manufactured the bottom logic die inside its own memory fabs.
With HBM4 doubling the interface to 2,048 bits, customers want custom logic etched on foundry nodes.
So SK Hynix partnered with TSMC to fabricate HBM4 base dies, blurring memory into custom silicon.
Meanwhile, Samsung owns both memory fabs and logic foundries under one roof if it fixes yields.

long_scenes.narration: And unlike commodity DDR RAM, custom-bonded HBM4 towers cannot be dumped onto spot markets if AI cools.
In 2013, SK Hynix escaped the commodity trap by building a chip tailored for one bold partner.
Today, that exact specialization gives SK Hynix the keys to the AI kingdom.
And ties its entire future to keeping that crown one microscopic layer ahead of everyone else.

sources.title: Wikipedia — High Bandwidth Memory
sources.summary: High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) is a computer memory interface for 3D-stacked synchronous dynamic random-access memory (SDRAM), initially developed by Samsung, AMD and SK Hynix. It is often used in conjunction with performance-oriented graphics accelerators, network devices, FPGAs and ASICs; some CPUs use HBM as on-package cache or RAM, such as the NEC SX-Aurora TSUBASA and Fujitsu A64FX. The first HBM memory chip was produced by SK Hynix in 2013, and the first devices shipped with HBM were the AMD Fiji GPUs in 2015. HBM was adopted by JEDEC as an industry standard in October 2013. The second generation, HBM2, was accepted by JEDEC in January 2016. JEDEC officially announced the HBM3 standard on January 27, 2022, and the HBM4 standard in April 2025. In 2025, the world's largest manufacturers of HBM include SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, and Micron Technology. TSMC produces the base die for HBM and is planned to be the foundry for several HBM companies in 2026. HBM has had an unprecedented demand increase, and in general DRAM (DDR4, DDR, and flash memory/NAND) price has in early 2026 "experienced compounded increases, some exceeding 200%, since early 2025 ... sources.title: Wikipedia — Memory bandwidth
sources.summary: Memory bandwidth is the rate at which data can be read from or stored into a semiconductor memory by a processor. Memory bandwidth is usually expressed in units of bytes/second, though this can vary for systems with natural data sizes that are not a multiple of the commonly used 8-bit bytes. Memory bandwidth that is advertised for a given memory or system is usually the maximum theoretical bandwidth. In practice the observed memory bandwidth will be less than (and is guaranteed not to exceed) the advertised bandwidth. A variety of computer benchmarks exist to measure sustained memory bandwidth using a variety of access patterns. These are intended to provide insight into the memory bandwidth that a system should sustain on various classes of real applications. == Measurement conventions == There are three different conventions for defining the quantity of data transferred in the numerator of "bytes/second": The bcopy convention: counts the amount of data copied from one location in memory to another location per unit time. For example, copying 1 million bytes from one location in memory to another location in memory in one second would be counted as 1 million bytes per second....

sources.summary: SK Hynix Inc. (Korean: 에스케이하이닉스 주식회사), stylized SK hynix, is a South Korean semiconductor company that manufactures dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) chips and flash memory chips. SK Hynix is one of the world's largest semiconductor vendors, and, along with Samsung Electronics and Micron, one of the "Big Three" memory manufacturers. Founded in 1983 as Hyundai Electronics, SK Hynix was integrated into the SK Group in 2012 following a series of mergers, acquisitions, and restructuring efforts. After being incorporated into the SK Group, SK Hynix became a major affiliate alongside SK Innovation and SK Telecom. The company's major customers include Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Asus, Dell, MSI, HP Inc., and Hewlett Packard Enterprise (formerly Hewlett-Packard). sources.title: Wikipedia — Advanced packaging
sources.summary: Advanced packaging is the aggregation and interconnection of components before traditional integrated circuit packaging, where a single die is packaged. Advanced packaging allows multiple devices, including electrical, mechanical, or semiconductor devices, to be merged and packaged as a single electronic device. Advanced packaging uses processes and techniques that are typically performed at semiconductor fabrication facilities, unlike traditional integrated circuit packaging, which does not. Advanced packaging thus sits between fabrication and traditional packaging-or, in other terminology, between BEoL and post-fab. Advanced packaging includes multi-chip modules, 3D ICs, 2.5D ICs, heterogeneous integration, fan-out wafer-level packaging, system-in-package, quilt packaging, combining logic (processors) and memory in a single package, die stacking, wafer bonding/stacking, several chiplets or dies in a package, combinations of these techniques, and others. 2.5D and 3D ICs are also called 2.5D or 3D packages. sources.title: Benchmarking High Bandwidth Memory on FPGAs (Zeke Wang, Hongjing Huang, Jie Zhang)
sources.summary: FPGAs are starting to be enhanced with High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) as a way to reduce the memory bandwidth bottleneck encountered in some applications and to give the FPGA more capacity to deal with application state. However, the performance characteristics of HBM are still not well specified, especially in the context of FPGAs. In this paper, we bridge the gap between nominal specifications and actual performance by benchmarkingHBM on a state-of-the-art FPGA, i.e., a Xilinx Alveo U280 featuring a two-stack HBM subsystem. To this end, we propose Shuhai, a benchmarking tool that allows us to demystify all the underlying details of HBM on an FPGA. FPGA-based benchmarking should also provide a more accurate picture of HBM than doing so on CPUs/GPUs, since CPUs/GPUs are noisier systems due to their complex control logic and cache hierarchy. Since the memory itself is complex, leveraging custom hardware logic to benchmark inside an FPGA provides more details as well as accurate and deterministic measurements. We observe that 1) HBM is able to provide up to 425GB/s memory bandwidth, and 2) how HBM is used has a significant impact on performance, which in turn demonstrates the importance
key_facts: We observe that 1) HBM is able to provide up to 425GB/s memory bandwidth, and 2) how HBM is used has a significant impact on performance, which in turn demonstrates the importance of unveiling the performance characteristics of HBM so as to select the best approach.

sources.title: High Bandwidth Memory on FPGAs: A Data Analytics Perspective (Kaan Kara, Christoph Hagleitner, Dionysios Diamantopoulos)
sources.summary: FPGA-based data processing in datacenters is increasing in popularity due to the demands of modern workloads and the ensuing necessity for specialization in hardware. Driven by this trend, vendors are rapidly adapting reconfigurable devices to suit data and compute intensive workloads. Inclusion of High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) in FPGA devices is a recent example. HBM promises overcoming the bandwidth bottleneck, faced often by FPGA-based accelerators due to their throughput oriented design. In this paper, we study the usage and benefits of HBM on FPGAs from a data analytics perspective. We consider three workloads that are often performed in analytics oriented databases and implement them on FPGA showing in which cases they benefit from HBM: range selection, hash join, and stochastic gradient descent for linear model training. We integrate our designs into a columnar database (MonetDB) and show the trade-offs arising from the integration related to data movement and partitioning. In certain cases, FPGA+HBM based solutions are able to surpass the highest performance provided by either a 2-socket POWER9 system or a 14-core XeonE5 by up to 1.8x (selection), 12.9x (join), and 3.2x (SGD)
key_facts: In certain cases, FPGA+HBM based solutions are able to surpass the highest performance provided by either a 2-socket POWER9 system or a 14-core XeonE5 by up to 1.8x (selection), 12.9x (join), and 3.2x (SGD).
